title: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it
description: OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with
body: OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so. An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks."In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post. Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech. The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks.OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.

schema.headline: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it

title: Japan exports post huge miss in September as growth slows to 16.7%
description: IBARAKI, JAPAN - JUNE 17:  Technicians at work in the clean room of the Fab Equipment at a semiconductor company, Renesas Technology Corp. on June 17,
body: IBARAKI, JAPAN - JUNE 17:  Technicians at work in the clean room of the Fab Equipment at a semiconductor company, Renesas Technology Corp. on June 17, 2004 in Ibaraki, Japan. Renesas is the first company to produce semiconductor products from 300mm wafer in the world. (Photo by Koichi Kamoshida/Getty Images)Koichi Kamoshida | Getty Images Entertainment | Getty ImagesJapan's exports in September rose 16.7% from a year earlier, missing market expectations by a huge margin. Reuters-polled analysts had pegged exports growth at 20.1%.This is the second straight month that shipments from Japan have recorded a slowdown, after hitting a near four-year high in July. Growth was supported by continued strong semiconductor exports, with shipments rising 49.4% year on year by value. Exports of machinery also bolstered growth, with semiconductor-related machinery shipments up 43.9% and power generation machinery exports climbing 22.6%.In terms of destinations, shipments to mainland China — Japan's largest trading partner — rose 8.6%, while exports to the U.S. climbed 22.9%.Exports have been the main driver of Japan's growth for the first two quarters of 2026, helping the world's fourth largest economy beat expectations in the first quarter, and supporting growth in the second.Japan's imports in September grew 18.9%, also missing expectations of 19.6% from Reuters. Tokyo's imports of petroleum climbed 51.1% by value in September, with inbound shipments from the U.S. surging nearly 820%, while those from the Middle East inching up just 1.5% as the conflict in the region continues to impede supplies.Following the data release, the benchmark Nikkei 225 was up 1.8%, while the Topix gained 1.14%. The data comes as the Bank of Japan is set to meet next week, and Reuters poll estimates indicate that the central bank is set to hold its policy rate steady at 1%.

schema.headline: Japan exports post huge miss in September as growth slows to 16.7%

title: Anthropic in talks with neocloud Nscale over second multibillion-dollar deal, source tells CNBC
description: Anthropic is in talks with U.K. neocloud Nscale for a second multibillion-dollar deal to lease computing capacity at a site in the U.S., a person fami
body: Anthropic is in talks with U.K. neocloud Nscale for a second multibillion-dollar deal to lease computing capacity at a site in the U.S., a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.The agreement would cover a second 460-megawatt data center at the same West Virginia site as the first deal, the person said. The person asked not to be named because they were not authorized to discuss the talks. The deal could be worth around $45 billion, the person said.CNBC reported the first deal in August.Bloomberg first reported that Anthropic and Nscale were in talks over a second deal. Anthropic declined to comment. Nscale has been approached for comment.AI infrastructure faces headwindsNvidia-backed Nscale is one of several companies that have emerged in recent years to develop the infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence. The company builds or leases data centers and sells computing capacity to hyperscalers and AI labs.Rivals CoreWeave and Nebius have seen their shares drop 28% and 27%, respectively, in the past month, amid concerns over heavy borrowing.Nscale has faced its own challenges. On Sunday, U.K. newspaper The Telegraph reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid.An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site.""Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," the spokesperson added.The U.K.-based company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange in September.Anthropic's computing pushAnthropic said earlier this year that growing demand for its Claude AI models and products has caused "inevitable strain" on its infrastructure. Since then, it has announced a flurry of deals with infrastructure partners to try and increase its computing capacity, including major agreements with Advanced Micro Devices, Elon Musk's SpaceX, Google and  Broadcom.

schema.headline: Anthropic in talks with neocloud Nscale over second multibillion-dollar deal, source tells CNBC

title: Prediction-market odds rise for Marine Le Pen in France 2027 presidential race as protests roil nation
description: A protester waving a French national flag walks past a fire during clashes prior to the start of a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of
body: A protester waving a French national flag walks past a fire during clashes prior to the start of a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of living", in Marseille, southern France, on Oct. 17, 2026.Thibaud Moritz | AFP | Getty ImagesAs protests intensify in France, Kalshi traders see a growing likelihood that far-right candidate Marine Le Pen will win that country's presidential race in 2027.Student-led protests first erupted in Paris over frustration with school conditions and teacher shortages in September but rippled into national outrage over the country's living costs and public services, including in education and healthcare. Authorities said over 500,000 people demonstrated nationwide over the weekend. Since the protests have started, Kalshi trading activity over who will be the next French president has jumped on Kalshi. Odds for far-right candidate Marine Le Pen have jumped to 53% from 39% in the last month. Just days after the protests began, speculators placed a 44.7% chance on Sept. 26 that David Lisnard, the current mayor of Cannes, would become the country's next president. Those odds came in just a day after he held a major campaign rally for the presidential race. Lisnard's Kalshi odds of winning the 2027 presidential contest dropped to 11% by Tuesday afternoon. The contract asks "Next French presidential election winner?" and will be verified by French government next year. Le Pen has repeatedly criticized the escalating civil unrest, cementing it as a key message in her campaign and arguing that leadership under Emmanuel Macron's centrist government has contributed to the conditions behind the protests."You saw yesterday our cities, our streets, our country, battered, mistreated, ransacked," Le Pen wrote in an Oct. 18 post on social media platform X, following some of the country's worst unrest in years, with over 2,000 arrests and nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes injured, according to the country's ministry. During the demonstration on 17 October in Limoges protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges Haute-Vienne in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region of France on 17 October 2026. Elise Cabane | Afp | Getty Images"We are living through a profound crisis of trust, of authority that poses a threat to democracy. This observation must alert us: our country is caught in a vise, or even taken hostage, between violence and powerlessness," Le Pen added. French stocks are also facing volatility, with the CAC 40 index down 2.8% in the last month and off almost 6% in the last six months. The country's bond yields, which measure the government's borrowing costs, have also been on the rise, with the 10-year government bond yield trading above 4.9%. "It will be difficult to see the budget deficit come down without painful measures," Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Prediction-market odds rise for Marine Le Pen in France 2027 presidential race as protests roil nation

title: Walmart launches joint membership with Sam's Club as it leans into delivery, gas discounts
description: Sam's Club and Walmart stores.Walmart on Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam's Club, as the r
body: Sam's Club and Walmart stores.Walmart on Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam's Club, as the retailer leans further into convenience and value to win over cash-strapped shoppers.The membership, which combines Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus, will cost $120 per year, according to the company. That price is nearly $100 less than buying individual annual memberships to each retailer, though there is no monthly payment option for the new deal. Both stores will continue to offer standalone options."We're giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement. "For $120 a year, we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own."The membership gives customers access to Sam's Club warehouses, free delivery from both chains, a subscription to Peacock or Paramount+ streaming services, gas savings and 2% Sam's Club cash on eligible purchases. Customers who already have accounts at both stores can link their accounts to receive the discount.While Walmart's customers often shop for routine, everyday essentials, Sam's Club warehouses offer more opportunity to stock up on bulk purchases. A joint membership could allow the store models to complement one another, according to the company.The announcement comes as Walmart bets on convenience to drive sales, especially as consumer wallets are squeezed by high gas and food prices. In August, as Walmart reported fiscal second-quarter earnings, the company raised its outlook for the year, with Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey telling CNBC that consumer spending remained strong despite higher fuel prices. Even so, its stock fell at the time as its sales outlook disappointed Wall Street. Rainey said in August that the company was lowering prices across various categories, including beef, adding that it's well positioned to weather economic uncertainty because of its emphasis on value and its scale.Meanwhile, Sam's Club saw a 26% increase in e-commerce sales in the fiscal second quarter, driven by increased transactions and membership growth. The retailer, which also operates its own gas stations, reported net sales of $25.7 billion, including fuel, during that period. The membership business — which is part of Walmart's push to grow sales with higher profit margins — is already strong. Walmart reported a 17% increase globally in revenue from its membership in the fiscal second quarter with Walmart+ net adds notching a record second-quarter high. For Sam's Club, that revenue number grew 6%.Walmart added Tuesday that employees at both stores will also receive joint memberships as part of their benefits. The company said any costs related to the changes in the membership program are not expected to materially impact the company's fiscal third-quarter or full-year guidance.

schema.headline: Walmart launches joint membership with Sam's Club as it leans into delivery, gas discounts

title: United Airlines slashes 2026 profit outlook on fuel prices, but travelers keep booking despite higher fares
description: A United Airlines Boeing 787 takes off from Heathrow Airport in London, March 31, 2026.Peter Nicholls | Getty ImagesUnited Airlines is slashing its pr
body: A United Airlines Boeing 787 takes off from Heathrow Airport in London, March 31, 2026.Peter Nicholls | Getty ImagesUnited Airlines is slashing its profit forecast for the year as fuel costs continue to bite, but the carrier said passengers keep booking.United said Tuesday that it expects to earn between 50 cents and $1.50 a share on an adjusted basis in the fourth quarter, well below the $1.76 a share Wall Street analysts expected. At the high end of that range, it would bring United's 2026 adjusted earnings to no more than $7.22 per share. In mid-July, United said it was expecting full-year earnings of $9 to $11 a share. The carrier expects to pay an average of $4.80 a gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from an average price of $3.90 a gallon in the third.A surge in fuel prices this year has added billions of dollars to airlines' costs, eating into profits, despite strong demand, and driving up airfares.Here is what United Airlines reported for the quarter that ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on estimates compiled by LSEG:Earnings per share: $2.54 adjusted vs. $2.57 expectedRevenue: $17.88 billion vs. $17.9 billion expectedUnited's third-quarter net income rose 8.5% from a year earlier to $1.03 billion, or $3.14 a share. During the same period last year its net income totaled $949 million, or $2.90 a share. "Our employees met the challenge of our ever-changing environment and our results prove the resilience of focusing on building a brand-loyal airline for customers," United CEO Scott Kirby said in an earnings release.United's fuel bill rose close to 62% in the quarter from a year earlier to $4.84 billion. Revenue for the three months ended Sept. 30 rose 17.4% from a year earlier to $17.88 billion, compared with $15.23 billion the year before.Domestic passenger unit revenue rose 14.5% from a year earlier, while international unit revenue was up 17.4%, a sign of higher fares. Passengers continue to book, United said, with passenger counts up more than 2% from last year.Adjusting for one-time items, United reported net income of $833 million or $2.54 a share.Read more CNBC airline newsWhy airfare could rise even more, but airline profits won’tBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to premium upgradesCompanies spurn airlines’ cheapest business class ticketsUnited’s next decision: What to do with all those Boeing 737 Max 10 seats it ordered years agoRecord heat, crowds drive offseason boom in international travel

schema.headline: United Airlines slashes 2026 profit outlook on fuel prices, but travelers keep booking despite higher fares

title: U.S. eyes refining muscle of Indian billionaire Ambani's Reliance as Rubio visits Jamnagar plant
description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during the Freedom 250 reception at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on October 20, 2026. Kylie Coop
body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during the Freedom 250 reception at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on October 20, 2026. Kylie Cooper | Afp | Getty ImagesU.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will discuss refining Western energy supplies with Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries when he visits the company's plant in Jamnagar, Gujarat — the world's largest single-site refinery.The U.S. is looking to "work together more closely" with Reliance for refining energy from the "Western Hemisphere," Rubio said in an interview with India's Network 18, which is owned by Reliance. "I think that's helpful to India, but it's also helpful to us," he added.Reliance's Jamnagar refinery, which Rubio will visit on Wednesday, has a crude processing capacity of 1.4 million barrels per day. Reliance has also emerged as the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude outside of the U.S., as of end-September.The company's "extraordinary" refining capacity could help India diversify its energy supplies, Rubio said, hinting at possibly greater offtake of Venezuelan crude."We think there's an opportunity for them [Reliance Industries] to continue to help India diversify its supply chain, its supply of energy," Rubio said, adding that Venezuela was ramping up energy production, and that "India has had a long history of being able to refine some of that."U.S. President Donald Trump has been pushing India to buy more Venezuelan oil to replace Russian barrels, and while state-owned oil companies are making opportunistic purchases, Reliance has been the primary buyer.'Refining Superpower'Beyond oil purchases, Reliance has been deepening ties with the U.S. this year, with Trump announcing in March that America will build its first new oil refinery in 50 years, helped by investment from Ambani's Reliance. While Reliance has not confirmed the size of investment, Trump in a Truth Social post had said that "THIS IS A HISTORIC $300 BILLION DOLLAR DEAL — THE BIGGEST IN U.S. HISTORY." Reliance has never made an announcement about the refinery investment, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC, adding that it creates an air of uncertainty around the deal. Rubio would seek to "clinch" that deal or take it a little further, Chaudhuri said. Rubio told Network 18 that Reliance had "invested in increasing the refining capacity within the United States."His visit to Jamnagar also comes at a time when diesel prices have surged in the U.S., with midterm elections looming. Diesel prices, which affect American truckers, farmers, and shippers, are expected to remain elevated going into next year. Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Rubio underscored Reliance's ability to refine heavy crude and referred to India as a "refining superpower" when asked about the role New Delhi and its companies can play in meeting the world's energy demand.Indian and Chinese refineries are good at handling heavy and medium-heavy crude from Venezuela and Russia, Chaudhuri said, adding that this grade of fuel is better-suited for producing diesel.

schema.headline: U.S. eyes refining muscle of Indian billionaire Ambani's Reliance as Rubio visits Jamnagar plant

title: Mike Bloomberg spent $80M to boost Democrats in midterms: NYT
description: Former Mayor of New York City Mike Bloomberg speaks at the opening session of the Qatar Economic Forum 2025 in Doha, Qatar, on May 20, 2025. Noushad T
body: Former Mayor of New York City Mike Bloomberg speaks at the opening session of the Qatar Economic Forum 2025 in Doha, Qatar, on May 20, 2025. Noushad Thekkayil | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesMike Bloomberg spent $80 million in September and October to help Democrats regain majority control of the House of Representatives in the upcoming midterm elections, The New York Times reported Tuesday, citing his team.Shortly after The Times published its article about Bloomberg's campaign spending, his fellow billionaire, President Donald Trump, in a social media post reiterated his vow to spend $400 million to boost Republican candidates.The dueling announcements came as Republicans are increasingly worried about retaining their majorities in both chambers of Congress.Many political analysts expect Democrats to win control of the House, and multiple polls show Democrats within reach of winning a majority of seats in the Senate.Bloomberg "is of the view that resources matter in campaigns," his political advisor Howard Wolfson told The Times.Bloomberg, a former New York City mayor, "expects a result," Wolfson said.With the $80 million in spending, Bloomberg is among the top five largest individual Democratic donors according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings for the 2025-2026 election cycle.Wolfson did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.Before Tuesday's announcement, Bloomberg was known to have donated $23 million to Democrats and affiliated causes this election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission records through Tuesday.As of the beginning of October, Bloomberg had put $11 million behind a super PAC supporting Micah Lasher in New York's 12th Congressional District and $2.5 million toward Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's reelection, according to campaign-finance records.Trump, in a Truth Social post, said that he and his affiliated political action committee have spent more than $300 million to help Republican candidates with advertising, voter contacts, rallies and turnout efforts. Trump promised that his spending will top $400 million by Election Day, Nov. 3.FEC filings as of Tuesday afternoon so far show roughly $200 million in identifiable spending and ad reservations tied to Trump's political operation, leaving a gap between what's publicly visible and Trump's broader claim.In September, Trump said he had "close to a billion dollars" in his super PAC, MAGA Inc., and planned to spend $400 million to $500 million on the midterms. At the time, MAGA Inc. reported about $403 million in cash on hand — less than half the amount Trump cited.

schema.headline: Mike Bloomberg spent $80M to boost Democrats in midterms: NYT

title: France to deploy military as it braces for fresh unrest this weekend
description: Protestors on the statue of Marianne on the Monument à la République (Statue de la République) during demonstrations on October 17, 2026 in Paris, Fra
body: Protestors on the statue of Marianne on the Monument à la République (Statue de la République) during demonstrations on October 17, 2026 in Paris, France. Carl Court | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesFrance will deploy some military forces to help maintain order during a fresh wave of protests expected this weekend, officials said Tuesday. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers in the National Assembly that the government would ⁠deploy forces from France's Sentinelle force — a domestic military operation that was launched in 2015 following terrorist attacks in Paris — "mainly on static security missions."This would free up police and gendarmes — a military police force — to carry out law enforcement objectives, Nuñez added.Also addressing parliament on Tuesday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said authorities planned to mobilize a "massive" security presence this coming Saturday, adding that the government's objective was to achieve "an immediate return to order."Lecornu also said there would be fresh curfews "where the situation requires it," according to French newspaper Le Monde. Curfews contributed to a "calm" night across France, he said earlier on Tuesday, even as public discontent remained high following the weekend's mass protests, looting and violent scenes. Certain areas of several French cities were under curfew overnight, including Place de la République and Les Halles in Paris, and parts of central Lyon. Lille and Nice were among the cities to impose curfews for minors.The unrest comes at a particularly fragile moment for France, where public anger over living costs and deteriorating services is colliding with political instability and a fiscal crisis that threatens to turn into a debt crisis as government borrowing costs rise to the highest level in decades.The country faces a divided parliament with no majority and presidential elections in April 2027.In a statement on Tuesday, Lecornu said local officials would impose new curfews where required. Meanwhile, criticism is mounting over President Emmanuel Macron's decision to embark on a three-day tour of the Middle East as France suffers its most severe riots in many years.Riots followed weeks of demonstrations over the country's education system, the cost of living and other issues.While hundreds of thousands of people marched peacefully, pockets of violence erupted, shocking the country, as protesters smashed shopfronts and set Limoges Town Hall on fire.Protesters vandalise a retail store during a demonstration near Paris's Place de la République, as the Gilets Jaunes join students for a weekend of action on Oct. 17, 2026 in Paris, France.Carl Court | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesPolitical commentator Christophe Barbier on radio station RTL said on Monday there was "no longer a pilot in the plane." At the same time, newspaper La Dépêche du Midi wrote in a scathing editorial that Macron had "to see if the misery of a reviled president is less painful in the Persian Gulf sun" as France "sinks deeper into crisis." Macron said on Sunday he was looking to address high fuel prices and secure French energy supplies through the trip to Kuwait, the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar, while strengthening defense and security cooperation.Businesses hitThere is also public anger over claims that police lost control of the situation at the weekend as disorder and looting escalated. Police were earlier this month accused of excessive force in their response to student protests, after a 15-year-old ​boy's hand was blown off by a stun grenade.Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez' offered to quit his post on Monday after claiming responsibility for what unfolded. Macron declined his resignation, saying immediate leadership of law enforcement was needed. "The lack of enforcement means that more than 3,000 shops have been sacked, and for the economy today we awake with a feeling that the state cannot do the basic duty that it is supposed to do, and this is now creating somehow lack of trust," Fabrice Le Saché, vice president of business group MEDEF, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday."This is dangerous because we have been used to... riots in our country — remember the Yellow Vests and other movements — but this one has passed, I think, the level of the previous ones, and we cannot continue to keep going with that same type of situation every time we have social unrest," Le Saché said.French businesses have one of the highest tax burdens in the euro area but now feel they cannot receive basic security in return, he added.Lecornu said Monday that a support fund would be established for damaged or looted businesses, and that the government would talk with insurers to speed up assessments. "The scale of the damage suggests this weekend's riots could ultimately prove more costly than the unrest that followed the death of Nahel Merzouk in 2023," which generated around 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion) in insured losses, Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft, said by email."Further violence is not inevitable, but protests linked to the underlying grievances, including cost-of-living pressures and discontent over public services and education, are likely to persist, putting continued pressure on the government to demonstrate that it can maintain order," Middleton said.French markets came under pressure on Monday after the weekend scenes, with bonds, stocks and the euro all selling off, amid growing skepticism about the country's ability to bring down its deficit to a sustainable level. Fierce debate is underway over the 2027 budget, with the government targeting an overall decline in the deficit to 5% of GDP from 5.4%.

schema.headline: France to deploy military as it braces for fresh unrest this weekend

title: Trump sued over 50% tariffs on Canada in latest trade challenge
description: U.S. President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn as he departs the White House on October 12, 2026 in Washington, DC.Aaron Schwartz | Getty ImagesA
body: U.S. President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn as he departs the White House on October 12, 2026 in Washington, DC.Aaron Schwartz | Getty ImagesA new lawsuit filed Tuesday challenges President Donald Trump's invocation of a Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.Trump in July used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap those steep tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, wigs, and other products in response to alleged trade discrimination by Ottawa. It was the first time the 96-year-old law had ever been used to impose a tariff."Section 338 is a relic of the retaliation-based tariff policy" that has been "impliedly repealed" by subsequent legislation, the civil complaint filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade says.The suit was filed by Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that says its cheeses are covered by the tariffs. The complaint asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, block their enforcement, and order the Trump administration to issue refunds for duties already paid, with interest.Gellert Global is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the same legal group that dealt a major blow to Trump's trade agenda by successfully contesting his "reciprocal" tariffs.The Supreme Court struck those tariffs down in February. The administration is in the process of refunding the estimated $166 billion that the federal government collected from importers through the reciprocal duties.The Liberty Justice Center is currently engaged in two other lawsuits against what it says is Trump's misuse of laws to impose sweeping tariffs. "This case is not about the president. It is about the presidency," the group's CEO Sara Albrecht said in a statement Tuesday morning announcing Gellert Global's suit. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required."The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the suit.Trump on July 20 signed three presidential proclamations targeting different sets of Canadian imports with the Section 338 tariffs in response to alleged unfair treatment in the U.S. motor vehicle, alcohol and dairy sectors.The tariffs took effect Aug. 22, after last-ditch trade talks with Canadian officials in Washington fell apart. Canada later retaliated with "dollar for dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods.Tuesday's lawsuit argues that even if the 1930 tariff law is upheld, the Trump administration did not meet the legislation's requirements when it imposed the duties on Canada. It says that the law permits tariff action "only upon finding 'as a fact'" that a foreign country is unequally imposing unreasonable charges or trade limitations on U.S. products, or that its customs rules otherwise unfairly disadvantage the U.S."Even then, the President may impose only such duties 'as he shall determine will offset such burden or disadvantage,'" the lawsuit states. But the Canadian actions cited in Trump's proclamations "do not discriminate against the United States," it says.Two of those actions are "Canada's responses to the President's own tariffs, including tariffs the Supreme Court has held unlawful, and retaliation is not discrimination," the lawsuit contends.Another centers on dairy quota terms that were negotiated in USMCA, the U.S.'s trilateral trade deal with Canada and Mexico. Those terms "give American cheese better access to Canada than the cheese of most of the world receives," the suit states.The suit says Gellert Global boasts more than $1.7 billion in annual revenue. In 2025, the company imported $71 million worth of Canadian cheese — including sheep's and goat's milk cheese, mascarpone, brie, camembert and the hybrid cheese borgonzola, the complaint says.Gellert says it paid no tariffs on its imports of Canadian cheese under USMCA. The Trump administration said in July that it would not renew that trade pact for another 16-year term.  Under the Section 338 tariffs, "Gellert now pays a 50 percent duty on the entered value of its Canadian cheese, an estimated $40 million per year," according to the suit.While it plans to absorb the costs through the end of the year, the situation is "not sustainable long term," the company says."If the tariffs continue, Gellert will be forced to raise the prices on its products, resulting in lost or reduced sales, decreased customer loyalty, risk of losing product placements due to higher costs, and supply chain interruptions as producers scale down or go out of business due to increased costs," the suit says.

schema.headline: Trump sued over 50% tariffs on Canada in latest trade challenge

title: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% — cementing rate hike expectations
description: A person shields themselves from the rain while walking near the Bank of England building on the day the Monetary Policy Committee lowered interest ra
body: A person shields themselves from the rain while walking near the Bank of England building on the day the Monetary Policy Committee lowered interest rates, in London, Britain, Dec.18, 2025. Toby Melville | ReutersU.K. inflation rose by a hotter-than-expected 3.5% in the 12 months to September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels. Economists polled by Reuters had been forecasting an annual inflation rate of 3.4%. September's print marked a continuation of the U.K.'s upward trend for inflation, which came in at 3.1% in August and 2.9% in July. The September reading was the highest annual inflation figure in almost a year. The U.K.'s Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday that the motor fuel inflation rate had hit its highest level since August 2022, when fuel costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Britain is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks, such as the U.S.-Iran war and the subsequent struggle to move oil through the Strait of Hormuz. U.K. motor fuel prices surged 29.8% in the year to September, ONS data showed on Wednesday. The British pound was flat against both the euro and the U.S. dollar following the data release, and yields on U.K. government bonds were also little changed. Scott Gardner, investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, said in a note Wednesday morning that recent growth in headline inflation had "undone the progress we saw in the spring.""Bank of England policymakers will be looking beyond the headline figure," he said. "Services inflation, in particular, has accelerated in recent months which will create concern that we are starting to see second round inflationary effects beyond energy prices. While we face a different set of challenges compared to 2021, the prolonged conflict is weighing on the U.K. economy and making the case for a rate hike stronger."Markets are pricing in a 98% chance that the Bank of England raises its key interest rate by 25 basis points to 4% next month, according to LSEG data, with the majority of traders also pricing in a further hike of the same size at the central bank's final meeting of the year in December. Budget headache Wednesday's expected rise in inflation also complicates the fiscal picture for the U.K. government and its finance minister.  Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is set to unveil his first fiscal shakeup next week during the U.K.'s hotly anticipated Autumn Budget. He is tasked with sticking to the previous government's so-called fiscal rules, which aim to rein in public debt while delivering on promises to soften the blow of surging consumer costs.But separate data published Wednesday showed the U.K.'s national debt was estimated to have exceeded £3 trillion ($4 trillion) in September for the first time. The cost of servicing those debts has risen drastically over the past year, and the British economy is struggling to grow. Healey said in a statement following Wednesday's data release that he would be "maintaining our fiscal discipline" in the budget next week, while working to "drive for growth [and give] businesses and families some breathing space."Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, said in a note Wednesday morning that rising inflation is turning the Autumn Budget into "a perilous high-wire act for the Chancellor."He said surging prices were "increasing pressure for cost-of-living support while pushing up government borrowing costs, which is shrinking fiscal headroom and narrowing his policy options." "With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise," he said. "Policymakers will also be looking to the Chancellor to avoid adding fuel to the inflation fire by delivering a credible, fiscally disciplined Budget."

schema.headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% — cementing rate hike expectations

title: Elon Musk ordered Starlink slowdown for Ukraine: Report
description: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a press briefing held by President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outsid
body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a press briefing held by President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026.Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesElon Musk ordered the slowdown of a version of SpaceX's Starlink that Ukraine has relied on in its war against Russia, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter.Musk, SpaceX's founder and CEO, last week "capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network," the Journal reported. The decision left some Ukrainian drones virtually inoperable, according to the newspaper.Musk and President Donald Trump, who have both recently criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, discussed the move to throttle Starlink "soon after" the change first became public last week, two people told the Journal.One of the people who spoke with the news outlet claimed that Musk discussed the matter with multiple senior Trump administration officials, including the president himself, prior to imposing the Starlink speed cap.The White House and an email associated with Musk did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the Journal's report, which was published minutes after SpaceX reported its latest quarterly earnings.The Journal's story was not mentioned in a subsequent conference call with Musk and investors.Trump said Monday that he did not know who ordered the Starlink interruption, "But I'd like to find out."The Journal reported that Zelenskyy's public complaints that the slowdown weakens Ukraine's defenses against Russian attacks led to an informal investigation within the White House.Last Wednesday, Musk wrote on X that Starshield systems, the military-grade version of Starlink, are "owned and controlled by the US government" and that any speed or usage limits are "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."

schema.headline: Elon Musk ordered Starlink slowdown for Ukraine: Report

title: Oil prices climb as traders assess Middle East developments
description: Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 09, 20
body: Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 09, 2026.Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesOil prices climbed Wednesday as worries over Middle East supply disruptions keep the market on edge, with attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy facilities denting sentiment.Brent crude futures gained 0.86% to $109.73 a barrel as of 3:33 a.m. ET, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 0.78%  to $98.58 a barrel.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBrent crude prices this yearIran's Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that naval mines had prevented three tankers attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz using routes Tehran deemed unauthorized."Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," IRGC said in a statement published on their official Sepah News website.Adding to regional worries, Yemen's Houthi militants claimed responsibility on Monday for strikes targeting Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and airports in Riyadh and Abha. The escalating tensions have also sent global oil shipping costs soaring, adding another layer of pressure to energy markets.The global average crude freight rate has surged above $20 per barrel, compared with just $3 a year earlier, according to a Goldman Sachs report published Tuesday. While rates have eased slightly in recent days, they remain roughly seven times higher than a year ago.Goldman estimated that war-risk premiums associated with crossing the Strait of Hormuz accounted for about $7 of the $20 year-on-year increase in average crude freight rates, while ship-to-ship transfers outside the Persian Gulf contributed another $4.The investment bank warned that elevated shipping costs could widen price differences between crude grades, squeeze refiners' profit margins and ultimately push up refined fuel prices."High freight costs have weighed particularly heavily on Asian refineries' net margins, threatening their refined product output, which could then raise global refined product prices," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote.

schema.headline: Oil prices climb as traders assess Middle East developments

title: Treasury yields steady as investors await jobless claims, mortgage data
description: Treasury yields steadied early on Wednesday as investors awaited fresh data for insights into the U.S. economic picture ahead of next week's Federal R
body: Treasury yields steadied early on Wednesday as investors awaited fresh data for insights into the U.S. economic picture ahead of next week's Federal Reserve interest rate decision.Yields on 10-year U.S. Treasurys — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — were unchanged at 5.1211%.The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, was holding firm at 4.7889%.  The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which often moves on geopolitical developments — also held steady at 5.4320%.One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.With the Federal Reserve's next interest rate meeting scheduled for Oct. 28, traders are weighing up how domestic economic data and global geopolitical developments are shaping the outlook for inflation and interest rates.Energy prices ticked higher Wednesday, with U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures up 0.86% at $98.66 per barrel, as fresh missile strikes on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy facilities sparked renewed concerns over oil supplies.The latest weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate is due out later from the Mortgage Bankers Association. Previously, the fixed-rate loan average moved 1 basis point higher to 7.5% in the week ended Oct. 9.That's followed Thursday by the Labor Department's initial jobless claims data for the week ending Oct. 17. The number of people claiming unemployment benefits rose slightly by 1,000 to 199,000 in the week ending Oct. 10.

schema.headline: Treasury yields steady as investors await jobless claims, mortgage data

title: Australian data center operator NextDC's shares plunge 40% after it slashes earnings forecast
description: The logo of Australian data centre operator NextDC is seen on its Artarmon facility in Sydney on September 15, 2026. (Photo by Saeed KHAN / AFP via Ge
body: The logo of Australian data centre operator NextDC is seen on its Artarmon facility in Sydney on September 15, 2026. (Photo by Saeed KHAN / AFP via Getty Images)Saeed Khan | Afp | Getty ImagesShares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast, citing power supply delays at its Melbourne facility amid local community and stakeholder opposition.The company lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to between $475 million Australian dollars and A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million forecast earlier, while cutting its underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, forecast to A$245 million to A$265 million from A$385 million to A$410 million. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconShares of NEXTDC on 22 Oct.The delays to power stem from the suspension of infrastructure upgrades at the company's M3 Melbourne data center amid community opposition, with electricity distributor Jemena not expecting to resume work before February 2027, according to NextDC.Jemena cited safety concerns and restricted access to work sites due to community opposition, as well as a lack of consent from the local council pending further community consultation.Citi said in a note that NextDC's power delays could affect earnings beyond fiscal 2027, citing delays to approvals for the M3 expansion and a longer-than-expected timeline for transformer upgrades.watch nowAs Australia grapples with growing concerns over the impact of data center developments on local communities, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government was working to establish national standards for investment.Chalmers told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Wednesday that the government welcomes investment in data centers and AI infrastructure, provided it aligns with the country's national interest, adding that the government was finalizing national investment standards to address concerns surrounding AI deployment. Australia is not alone in facing opposition to data center projects, there has been growing push back against data center developments worldwide, amid concerns over their impact on local communities and the environment.NextDC shares have declined for seven straight weeks, and are on course to end lower for the eighth week.

schema.headline: Australian data center operator NextDC's shares plunge 40% after it slashes earnings forecast
